title: Persuasive writing tricks that win readers over

steps.ask: How do I start a persuasive piece?

steps.label: Call to action

explain.say: Imagine your town wants to turn your favourite park into a car park. Oh no! You can write a letter to change their minds. That is persuasive writing. Look at the checklist on the board. First tick: say your opinion clearly. Our park must be saved!

explain.say: Next, back it up with facts and numbers. See the second tick? 300 children play there every week. Facts make people trust you. What fact could you use about your own school?

explain.say: Now a clever trick: a rhetorical question, a question you ask to make people think, not to get an answer. Look at the third tick: Where else will our children play? Can you feel how it pulls you in?

explain.say: See the next two ticks? Emotive words stir feelings: precious, peaceful, heartbreaking. And the rule of three: safe, green and free. Three ideas in a row sound strong and stick in the mind. Can you make your own three?

explain.say: Last tick: the call to action. Tell your reader exactly what to do: Sign our letter today! Superb, you now have a persuasive toolkit. Challenge: persuade me why your school should have a longer break, using three tricks.

faq.q: How do I start a persuasive piece?
faq.a: Start by stating your opinion clearly in the first sentence, like Our park must be saved, so the reader knows what you want.
A rhetorical question is asked to make the reader think, not to get an answer. Do we really want a town with no trees?

faq.q: What is a call to action?
faq.a: A call to action tells the reader exactly what to do next, like Sign the petition, Write to the council or Join us on Saturday.
asks: How do I end a persuasive letter?

faq.a: Emotive language uses words that make the reader feel something strongly, like heartbreaking, precious or shocking.

faq.q: What is the rule of three?
faq.a: The rule of three groups three words or ideas together, like safe, green and free. Three sounds complete and is easy to remember.

facts: Ancient Greek thinker Aristotle described three ways to persuade: by trust, by feelings and by reason.
The rule of three is common in famous speeches and slogans.
